blocks.content: SEBI operates as a quasi-judicial, quasi-legislative, and quasi-executive body to protect the interests of investors in securities and to promote the development of, and to regulate, the securities market.

rows: Drafts regulations and framing policy guidelines for market conduct
Framing SEBI (LODR) Regulations and Insider Trading Regulations
Conducts inspections, summons witnesses, and investigates market misconduct
Inspecting books of accounts of brokers or auditing listed entities
Adjudicates disputes, passes enforcement orders, and imposes monetary penalties
Issuing penalty orders for market manipulation or insider trading

items: Appeals against SEBI orders must be filed with the Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT) within 45 days from the date of receipt of the order.
SEBI cannot directly award imprisonment; criminal prosecution for non-compliance must be initiated before designated Special Courts.
Section 11(4) empowers SEBI to pass interim or final orders to restrain persons from accessing the securities market and freeze bank accounts during investigations.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: SEBI derives its core statutory powers from Section 11 of the SEBI Act, 1992 to protect investor interests and regulate the securities market.
SEBI exercises a triple role: Quasi-Legislative (drafting regulations), Quasi-Executive (investigation and inspection), and Quasi-Judicial (adjudication and passing penalty orders).
Under Section 11B, SEBI possesses broad powers to issue directions to any stock exchange, intermediary, or market participant in the interest of investors.
SEBI has the power to inspect books, summon persons, compel production of documents, and perform search and seizure operations with judicial magistrate authorization.
An appeal against any order passed by SEBI or an Adjudicating Officer lies with the Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT).
